note: Blueprint area: Drugs and alcohol (25% of the knowledge test). Drawn from Section B Chapter 7 (PDF pp.93-98) and the restricted-license material in Chapter B-8. The manual states that at least 25 percent of test questions come from this chapter, so it is weighted accordingly.

questions.stem: About how much alcohol can the liver oxidize in an hour?
options: It depends entirely on body weight
questions.explanation: The liver works at a fixed rate of roughly one drink an hour. Body weight changes how high your BAC climbs, but not how fast it falls.

questions.stem: Coffee, a cold shower or exercise will:
options: Speed up the rate at which alcohol leaves the body
Do nothing to speed up sobering — only time will
Lower blood alcohol concentration by about half
questions.explanation: These tricks may make a drinker feel more awake, but the alcohol is still in the blood. Only time sobers someone up.

questions.stem: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) measures:
options: The number of drinks consumed in the last hour
The percentage of alcohol in the blood
How long it has been since the last drink
questions.explanation: BAC is a percentage of alcohol in the blood, and impairment climbs as that number climbs.

questions.stem: In Tennessee, the blood alcohol concentration that is always illegal for a driver 21 or older is:
questions.explanation: Point-oh-eight is the line above which intoxication is illegal in Tennessee and most other states — but a driver can be convicted below it.

questions.stem: The first ability alcohol affects is:
questions.explanation: Judgment goes first, which is exactly why an impaired driver is a poor judge of whether they are impaired.

questions.stem: Alcohol, in any concentration, is:
options: A stimulant at low doses and a depressant at high doses
questions.explanation: It is a depressant at every concentration. Feeling lively after a drink is loss of inhibition, not stimulation.

questions.stem: Alcohol reduces the ability to see clearly at night by:
questions.explanation: Night vision is more than halved, and glare recovery slows too — which is why drinking and night driving is such a bad combination.

questions.stem: At a BAC of .05 percent, side vision is reduced by about:
questions.explanation: Losing roughly a third of your side vision means missing the cross traffic, the cyclist and the child at the curb.

questions.stem: Reaction time and coordination begin to be impaired at a BAC as low as:
questions.explanation: Impairment starts far below the legal limit — about one drink's worth for many people.

questions.stem: According to the manual, driving skills, judgment and vision are already greatly impaired at BAC levels as low as:
questions.explanation: Well under the legal limit. The manual also states flatly that everyone at .10 percent is too impaired to drive safely.

questions.stem: At a BAC of .10 percent, a driver is about how much more likely to cause a crash than a sober driver?
questions.explanation: Seven times at .10, twenty-five times at .15, and fifty times at .17 — the risk does not rise gently, it explodes.

questions.stem: The alcohol in one 12-ounce bottle of beer is about the same as the alcohol in:
questions.explanation: Beer, wine and spirits are served in different sizes precisely because their strength differs. A drink is a drink.

questions.stem: About how long does it take to cancel the intoxicating effects of one drink?
questions.explanation: One hour per drink. Three drinks, three hours — and no shortcut shortens it.

questions.stem: About what share of the information a driver uses comes from the eyes?
questions.explanation: Nearly everything you use to drive comes in through your eyes, so anything that degrades vision — alcohol, glare, fog — degrades driving.

questions.stem: A driver who has been drinking takes unnecessary risks such as speeding around curves or passing without enough clear distance. This is mainly a failure of:
questions.explanation: Alcohol lowers concern for physical wellbeing, so risks that would look obviously stupid sober start to look fine.

cite.quote: Good judgment decreases with the use of alcohol. The concern for physical well being also lessens. People under the influence of alcohol take unnecessary and dangerous risks.

questions.stem: The two abilities most important to driving, and most affected by small amounts of alcohol, are:
questions.explanation: Both are affected after a single drink, and both are the abilities driving depends on most.

cite.quote: The two abilities most important to the driving task are judgment and vision, both of which are affected by small amounts of alcohol.

questions.stem: Alcohol affects a driver's ability to judge:
questions.explanation: All three go together, and all three are altered after a single drink — which is why gaps look bigger and closing speeds look slower.

cite.quote: Your ability to judge speed, time and distance are altered after only one drink.

questions.stem: Glare vision and glare recovery in a drinking driver are:
options: Made worse, because eye muscles relax and recovery slows
questions.explanation: Relaxed eye muscles cannot focus properly, and the eyes take longer to recover after oncoming headlights — a longer stretch of driving effectively blind.

cite.quote: Glare vision is poor because of relaxed eye muscles. Glare recovery is also slowed by alcohol.

questions.stem: In Tennessee it is unlawful to drive or be in physical control of a vehicle while under the influence of:
options: Any intoxicant, marijuana, narcotic drug or stimulant drug
Only substances that are illegal to possess
questions.explanation: The DUI statute covers any intoxicant that impairs you, whether it came from a bar, a dealer or a pharmacy.

questions.stem: A driver who registers a BAC of .00 percent:
options: Can still be convicted of DUI
Can only be charged with reckless driving
questions.explanation: DUI is about impairment, not just about a number. Drugs — including prescription drugs — impair without registering any alcohol at all.

questions.stem: A BAC reading below .08 percent means the driver:
options: Is not cleared — a driver can still be convicted
Will be charged only if there was a crash
questions.explanation: The manual says it plainly: a level below .08 does not clear a driver.

questions.stem: Having a valid prescription for a drug that impairs your driving is:
options: A complete defense to a DUI charge
No defense to driving under the influence of it
A defense only for a first offense
questions.explanation: A prescription makes possession legal. It does not make impaired driving legal.

questions.stem: Tennessee's Implied Consent Law means that by driving in this state you have already agreed to:
options: Be tested for alcohol or drug content when an officer has reasonable grounds
Waive your right to a hearing
questions.explanation: Your consent came with the driving privilege. The officer still needs reasonable grounds to believe you were driving impaired.

questions.stem: A driver who is placed under arrest and refuses the officer's request for a blood alcohol test will likely:
options: Have driving privileges suspended by the court for twelve months
Face no consequence, since the test is voluntary
Receive a written warning for a first refusal
questions.explanation: Refusal is its own violation of the implied consent law, and the likely penalty is a twelve-month suspension — separate from anything the DUI charge brings.

questions.stem: Tennessee's "No Refusal" law allows law enforcement to:
options: Arrest a driver without probable cause
Seek a search warrant for a blood sample from a suspected impaired driver
Suspend a license at the roadside without a court
questions.explanation: Refusing the test does not end the matter — officers can go to a judge for a warrant and take the sample anyway.

questions.stem: The implied consent test is administered at the request of:
options: Any citizen who witnessed the driving
A law enforcement officer with reasonable grounds to believe you were driving under the influence
questions.explanation: Reasonable grounds are the trigger — an officer cannot demand a test of a driver at random.

questions.stem: Tennessee's DUI law applies on public streets and highways, and also:
options: On shopping center, trailer park and apartment complex premises and other places frequented by the public
Only where a speed limit is posted
questions.explanation: Private parking lots that the public uses are covered. "I never left the parking lot" is not a defense.

cite.quote: on the premises of any shopping center, trailer park, apartment house complex, or any place frequented by the public

questions.stem: Under Tennessee law you can be charged with DUI when you are:
options: Driving or in physical control of the vehicle
Only when the vehicle is moving in traffic
questions.explanation: Physical control counts. Sitting behind the wheel of a running car while impaired can be enough.

cite.quote: it is unlawful for any person to drive or be in physical control of an automobile or other motor-driven vehicle on any public street, highway, road or alley

questions.stem: A person whose license is revoked for DUI and who then applies for a photo identification license will find that the ID:
options: Looks exactly like any other state ID
Must indicate that the person is a DUI offender
questions.explanation: The department is required to mark the ID. The credential itself carries the record.

questions.stem: As a condition of probation, a DUI conviction in Tennessee requires the offender to:
options: Perform litter pick-up for three eight-hour shifts wearing a vest identifying them as a drunk driver
Serve as a volunteer driving instructor
questions.explanation: Three eight-hour shifts of roadside litter removal, wearing a vest that says "I am a DRUNK DRIVER."

questions.stem: The manual states that alcohol-related questions make up what share of the knowledge test?
questions.explanation: A quarter of the test comes from the alcohol and drugs chapter — by law, not by custom.

questions.stem: A driver who has been drinking and is stopped by an officer with reasonable grounds may be asked for a test of:
questions.explanation: The DUI statute is written around the alcohol concentration of blood or breath, and implied consent covers testing for alcohol or drug content.

questions.stem: Restricted driving privileges after a conviction are NOT available to a driver whose latest offense is:
options: Vehicular assault or aggravated vehicular homicide
questions.explanation: The most serious impaired-driving offenses close the restricted-license door entirely, as does a prior DUI within ten years.

questions.stem: After the first year of a two-year revocation, a driver may apply for a restricted license if they:
options: Install an ignition interlock device for the remaining period of revocation
questions.explanation: The interlock buys back part of the revocation: it must stay on the vehicle for the rest of the revocation period.

questions.stem: The minimum jail time for a first DUI conviction in Tennessee is:
questions.explanation: Forty-eight hours is the floor for a first conviction, and the table sets a longer minimum where the BAC was very high.

questions.stem: The fine range for a first DUI conviction in Tennessee is:
questions.explanation: And that is only the fine — court costs, bond, attorney fees, treatment and insurance increases come on top.

cite.quote: 1st Conviction 2nd Conviction 3rd Conviction 4th or subsequent Conviction (is a Class E felony)
Jail Time Fines License Revocation Period Vehicle Seizure

questions.stem: The license revocation period for a first DUI conviction is:
questions.explanation: One year for a first conviction, two for a second, three to ten for a third.

cite.quote: 1st Conviction 2nd Conviction 3rd Conviction 4th or subsequent Conviction (is a Class E felony)
1 year 2 years 3 -10 years 5 years [to indefinite]
Jail Time Fines License Revocation Period Vehicle Seizure

questions.stem: On a second DUI conviction, the vehicle:
options: Is subject to seizure and forfeiture
Cannot be touched by the state
questions.explanation: From the second conviction on, the car itself is on the line.

questions.stem: A fourth or subsequent DUI conviction in Tennessee is:
options: Still a misdemeanor, with a larger fine
questions.explanation: It stops being a misdemeanor. A felony conviction carries consequences that outlast any driving penalty.

questions.stem: A driver's vehicle will be seized if the driver has:
options: Two DUI convictions within five years, both after January 1997
Three moving violations in a year
questions.explanation: Two convictions inside five years triggers seizure, provided both offenses happened after January 1997.

questions.stem: An ignition interlock device keeps a vehicle from starting when:
options: The driver's BAC is too high
The driver is not wearing a seat belt
The vehicle is overdue for inspection
questions.explanation: The driver blows into the device before the engine will start, and again at intervals while driving.

cite.quote: Only a motor vehicle equipped with a functioning ignition interlock device (which keeps a car from starting if the driver's BAC is too high).

questions.stem: The ignition interlock restriction for a first DUI offense can last:
questions.explanation: Six months to a year for a first offense, up to three years for a second, and up to ten years for a third or later.

questions.stem: A person with two DUIs in a five-year period must use an ignition interlock device for how long after reinstatement?
questions.explanation: The interlock stays on for six months after you get your privileges back — the restriction outlives the revocation.

questions.stem: Driving under the influence and causing a crash that kills another person may be charged as:
questions.explanation: Vehicular homicide carries fines and prison, and it is a permanent bar to a restricted license.

questions.stem: Driving under the influence and causing a crash that injures another person may be charged as:
questions.explanation: An injury crash turns an impaired-driving charge into a violent felony charge carrying fines and prison.

questions.stem: Under the Drunk Driving Child Protection Act, violating the DUI laws while a child under 18 is in the vehicle adds a mandatory minimum of:
options: 30 days in jail and a $1,000 fine
questions.explanation: Both penalties are mandatory minimums, and both are added on top of everything else the DUI carries.

questions.stem: If a child suffers serious bodily injury in a DUI crash, the violation is:
questions.explanation: A Class D felony for serious injury, and a Class C felony — especially aggravated child endangerment — if the child dies.

questions.stem: A driver whose privileges are already revoked for DUI and who is caught driving on that revoked license may have the vehicle:
questions.explanation: Driving on a DUI revocation puts the car itself at risk of seizure, first offense or not.

cite.quote: A vehicle can be seized if a driver is charged with driving on a revoked license when his/her driving privileges are already revoked as a result of a DUI conviction

questions.stem: In addition to jail and fines, a judge will require a DUI offender who had a prior DUI in the previous five years to:
options: Undergo a drug and alcohol treatment assessment and receive treatment as appropriate
questions.explanation: Repeat offenders are assessed and treated, not just punished — the court treats the drinking as the underlying problem.

cite.quote: To undergo a drug and alcohol treatment assessment and receive treatment, as appropriate, for those who have had a prior DUI in the five years prior to the current DUI.

questions.stem: Besides fines and court costs, the manual lists which of these as a real cost of a DUI?
questions.explanation: Bond, attorney fees, lost work, treatment fees and higher premiums add up to thousands of dollars beyond the fine.

cite.quote: increased insurance premiums, and other expenses. This can add up to several thousand dollars.

questions.stem: A DUI offender ordered into a restricted license must, in most cases, submit:
options: Two copies of the court order and proof of SR-22 insurance
A letter from an employer only
questions.explanation: Two copies of the court order, proof of financial responsibility, the required tests and the fees.

questions.stem: A restricted license issued after a DUI conviction may permit driving:
options: To and from work, full-time college and religious services
questions.explanation: The trial judge's order names the permitted trips — work, full-time college, worship and driving that is part of the job.

cite.quote: The restricted license permits the driver to operate a motor vehicle for very specific purposes that are spelled out when the license is issued.

DUI: After conviction for DUI, the trial judge may issue an order for a restricted license to go to and from work, attend college full time, attend religious services at their place of worship, drive as part of employment

questions.stem: A driver who is at least 16 but not yet 21 commits underage driving while impaired at a BAC of:
questions.explanation: Two hundredths of a percent — roughly one drink. Tennessee sets a much lower line for drivers under 21.

questions.stem: The penalty for underage driving while impaired includes:
options: Loss of license for one year and a $250 fine
questions.explanation: A year without a license and a $250 fine, sometimes with public service work attached.

questions.stem: A person 18, 19 or 20 years old who is convicted of purchasing or possessing alcohol loses the privilege to drive for:
options: Only until the fine is paid
questions.explanation: One year for a first conviction, two for a second — and it applies whether or not a vehicle was involved at all.

questions.stem: The alcohol-conviction suspension for an 18 to 20-year-old applies:
options: Only if the person was driving at the time
Whether or not the person was driving or even in a vehicle
Only if the person was in a parking lot
questions.explanation: It is a driving penalty attached to an alcohol conviction, not a driving offense. Buying a beer at 19 can cost a license.

questions.stem: A person between 13 and 17 found to have possessed, consumed or sold alcohol or drugs has driving privileges suspended for:
options: One year or until age 17, whichever is longer
questions.explanation: A second conviction stretches it to two years or until age 18, whichever is longer.

questions.stem: A second juvenile drug or alcohol conviction suspends driving privileges for:
options: Two years or until age 18, whichever is longer
questions.explanation: The suspensions stack toward adulthood — the second one runs to at least age 18.

questions.stem: A person under 18 may lose driving privileges for a drug or alcohol offense:
options: Only if it happened while driving
Whether or not the offense occurred while driving
questions.explanation: For drivers under 18 the offense does not have to touch a car at all.

cite.quote: In addition, persons under the age of 18 may lose their driving privileges for:

questions.stem: Everyday over-the-counter medicines such as cold remedies and antihistamines:
options: Can affect driving ability and should be checked before driving
Cancel out the effects of alcohol
questions.explanation: The manual treats "every day" drugs as a real hazard. Read the label, and never mix them with alcohol.

cite.quote: Even some over-the-counter medicines can affect driving.
If you have questions about a particular drug or combination of drugs, check with your doctor or pharmacist.

questions.stem: Combining a prescription or over-the-counter drug with alcohol:
options: Is safe as long as the dose is small
Can multiply the effect of both
questions.explanation: Mixing is where people get caught out: the combined effect is far larger than either substance alone.

cite.quote: when alcohol is combined with another depressant, like tranquilizers or sedatives, the results are not just added together; they are multiplied

questions.stem: Driving under the influence of an illegal drug in Tennessee carries:
options: The same penalties as driving under the influence of alcohol
questions.explanation: Same law, same penalties — and prescription drugs are treated the same way.

questions.stem: Possession by a driver of five or more grams of methamphetamine in a vehicle is:
options: A ground for revoking or suspending a Tennessee driver license
questions.explanation: It is item 17 on the manual's list of grounds for losing your license.

cite.quote: In Tennessee, a driver license may be revoked or suspended for the following situations:

questions.stem: The best plan for a driver who intends to drink is to:
options: Decide in advance not to drive and arrange another way home
Wait fifteen minutes after the last drink
questions.explanation: The manual's prevention advice is to plan before the first drink, because judgment is the first thing you lose.

cite.quote: If you are planning a night on the town, decide before you start drinking that you are not going to drive.

questions.stem: Riding as a passenger with a driver who has been drinking is:
options: Safe as long as you wear a belt
A serious danger the manual warns young people about specifically
questions.explanation: The manual singles this out: young people are endangered not only by their own impaired driving but by getting into a car with someone else who is impaired.

cite.quote: Young people remain especially vulnerable to the threat of alcohol and other drugs.
This is not only from their own impaired driving, but also from getting in the car with other drivers who are not sober.

questions.stem: Compared with older drivers, a young driver with a BAC between .01 and .08 percent has:
options: A much greater chance of a crash
About the same chance of a crash
A lower chance, because of faster reflexes
questions.explanation: Low tolerance and limited driving experience combine, so young drivers are in trouble at alcohol levels that would be under the adult limit.

cite.quote: The young driver's chance of a crash is much greater with BAC between .01-.08 percent than older drivers.
